title: The Second Desk
briefing:
Welch Tapman was found on Tuesday morning in his own rooms off Narcissus Street, seated at his desk, with the door bolted on the inside and no mark on him anywhere.

You know the posture. You were found in it, in this house, eight days ago, and the only difference is that somebody put a revolver in the account of you and nobody has yet explained where it came from.

Welch held a gathering. He read something aloud from a set of divination notes he had no business owning. You were there. The Nighthawks have the file because the Church takes an interest in men who die that way — and Captain Smith is giving it to the probationer whose own name is already in it.

objectives.text: Establish how the rooms were sealed
Put the evening to Kohler Fels
Learn what actually stopped his heart

clues.title: The door was bolted from within
clues.text: A heavy iron bolt, thrown across and still in its housing when the police broke the frame. No trick of string throws that from the landing.

clues.title: The shutters were nailed shut
clues.text: Every window shuttered and nailed from the inside, and the nail heads are bright. He did this in the last week. He was expecting something, and not through the door.

clues.title: No wound, and no poison
clues.text: No mark on him at all. The police surgeon looked twice because he did not believe himself the first time. A healthy man of twenty-six simply stopped, sitting upright, with his pen still in his hand.

clues.title: His watch stopped at 11:47
clues.text: Wound, undamaged, and stopped — not run down. The mainspring still has tension in it. Whatever reached this room reached the watch as well.

clues.title: Two cups, and only one drunk from
clues.text: Set out on the desk, both poured, one cold and full. Welch had company, and his company sat through whatever came next without touching the tea.

clues.title: A page cut out of the notebook
clues.text: The notes are bound in his own stitching, and one leaf has been cut close to the thread with something sharper than a penknife. The stubs of two words survive at the gutter. Neither is Loenese.

clues.title: Coal dust on the stair
clues.text: Tracked up from the cellar, dry, and laid down after the rain stopped at eight. Somebody came up out of that cellar late, and it was not Welch, whose boots are clean and by the bed.

clues.title: The cellar hatch is bolted from inside
clues.text: The yard hatch, the one way in that is not the stair, fastened from the cellar side. Whoever used it drew it shut behind him.

clues.title: His money was not touched
clues.text: Eleven pounds and some silver in an unlocked box on the shelf, in plain sight of the desk. Nobody who came here for money would have left that.

clues.title: Something clings to the pendulum
clues.text: A copper plumb on a waxed thread, lying where it fell. To an ordinary eye, a curiosity. To yours, it is still faintly warm in a way that has nothing to do with the fire, and it is still pointed at the chair.

clues.title: The room remembers being afraid
clues.text: Not his fear. Fear does not print itself on plaster from one man. This is the residue of a thing that was afraid of what it had been called into, and could not leave until it was finished.

clues.title: A second man waited in the cellar
clues.text: In the gap behind the crates: dust disturbed and then smoothed over, and the shape of somebody sitting with his back to the wall for a long time. Long enough to hear the whole of it through the floor.

clues.title: Naya will not describe the door
clues.text: She found him. She will tell you the hour, the weather and what she had eaten, in order, twice. Ask her about the door and she talks about the hour again.

clues.title: The police put it at midnight
clues.text: Sergeant Gehrman's report says the surgeon put death near midnight and that the sergeant saw no reason to write anything else, which is a different sentence from agreeing with it.

clues.title: The cathedral bell rang eleven
clues.text: The bell was heard from the landing that night by two neighbours, both certain, and both certain the light under Welch's door was already out — which cannot be true of a man who died at midnight.

clues.title: Kohler says he went home at nine
clues.text: Straight from the gathering to his lodgings across the Tussock, he says, and can name the two people he passed. He offers the detail before it is asked for.

clues.title: The last crossing is at seven
clues.text: There is no bridge for four miles and the ferry stops at seven. Anybody on the far bank at nine either swam or was never on the far bank.

clues.title: He did not cross that night
clues.text: Sil Mowbray worked the boat and remembers the fares, because there were four of them and he had hoped for more. Kohler Fels was not one.

clues.title: A collector was buying the page
clues.text: Mr. Aldous, who keeps a door in the lower market, was offering nine pounds for a single leaf out of a set of divination notes — by description, not by name. He stopped offering on the Wednesday.

deductions.title: Nothing left these rooms after they were shut
deductions.text: Door bolted, shutters nailed, hatch bolted. Every opening fastened from the inside. Whatever was in here when it was sealed was still in here.

deductions.title: Somebody sat out the rite in the cellar
deductions.text: Coal tracked up after the rain, a hollow behind the crates worn by a man's back, and the residue of a second presence under the floor. He waited, he listened, and he came up afterwards.

deductions.title: The rite finished, and it finished him
deductions.text: No wound, a room printed with a terror that was not his, and a pendulum still warm and still pointing at the chair. He read the page aloud and something came the length of the thread to answer it.

deductions.title: He died at a quarter to twelve, not at midnight
deductions.text: The watch stopped at 11:47 and two neighbours put his light out before the bell rang eleven. The surgeon's midnight is a rounding, and the quarter-hour it rounds away is the whole case.

deductions.title: Kohler cut the page out to sell it
deductions.text: One leaf taken close to the stitching, and a collector in the lower market buying exactly one leaf of exactly those notes, by description. He was not stealing a book. He was filling an order.

deductions.title: Kohler was in the house that night
deductions.text: Two cups poured and one untouched, and a crossing he could not have made. He did not go home at nine. He went down to the cellar and stayed.

deductions.title: Nobody came here for money
deductions.text: Eleven pounds in an open box a yard from the body, untouched — and Naya, who will describe everything in that room except the way out of it.

resolutions.label: Name Kohler Fels, and hand Smith the pendulum
resolutions.summary: The whole account: the cut page, the cellar, the buyer, and the thing on the end of the thread.
resolutions.epilogue:
You lay it out for Dunn Smith in the order a report wants it: the notebook first, then the ferry, then the cellar. He listens with his eyes shut and does not write a word, and at the end he says the number of the artifact you are holding before you have finished describing it.

Kohler confesses on his own doorstep, before anyone has finished asking. He says he only meant to take the page. He says he did not know it would answer. Watching his face, you believe him, and it does not help.

Old Neil seals the pendulum in lead and lime and signs it into the Church's cupboard. Smith says nothing at all about your part in it, which from him is the loudest approval available.

He does say one other thing, on the stairs, not looking at you: that a man who reads that page aloud dies at his desk, and that the report on the desk in this house eight days ago says revolver. And then he says goodnight.

resolutions.label: Take Kohler to the police and keep the rest
resolutions.summary: Enough for an arrest, and nothing the Church would have to act on.
resolutions.epilogue:
Gehrman takes him, because you have given him a man who cannot account for an evening and a ferryman who can. It will hold. It will also be written up as a robbery that frightened a man to death, which is a sentence that means nothing and will be filed for thirty years.

You keep the pendulum in your coat all the way home and are aware of it the entire way. Smith notices you are carrying something. Smith notices everything, and says nothing, and that is worse than being asked.

resolutions.label: Give the Church the rite and let the man go
resolutions.summary: The dangerous half, handed over whole. The man who sold the page walks.
resolutions.epilogue:
You bring in the pendulum, the notebook, and an account of the rite exact enough that Old Neil goes quiet halfway through copying it out. The Church would rather have this than a conviction, and says so.

Kohler Fels leaves Tingen on the Thursday coach. Naya asks you, on the landing, whether anyone is going to be held to account, and you find that the true answer — that a thing is, and it has been put in a lead box — is not one you can say to her.

resolutions.label: Sell what you know to Aldous
resolutions.summary: The buyer still wants the page. He would pay more for the man who cut it out.
resolutions.epilogue:
Aldous pays in old notes, counted twice, and asks no questions except one, which is where the rest of the notes are now. You do not answer it. He writes something down anyway.

The money settles the quarter and buys Melissa a term of books. You are aware, putting it on the table, that you have just become a man somebody keeps a page about — and that the last man who was that is why you live in this room.

resolutions.label: Report that you could not close it
resolutions.summary: No account, no arrest, no artifact.
resolutions.epilogue:
Smith takes it better than you had prepared for, which is its own kind of unpleasant. He says the first one is usually like this and asks whether you slept, and you say yes, and he writes that down.

The rooms off Narcissus Street are let again by the end of the month. Nobody nails the shutters.

leads.label: Ask along the Tussock wharf about the crossings
leads.description: Somebody on that river works every crossing there is. One of them will remember a fare, and all of them will remember the hours.
leads.successText: Three hands tell you the same thing without conferring, which is how you know it is a timetable and not an opinion: last boat at seven, no bridge for four miles, and a great deal of feeling about both.
leads.failureText: You buy two rounds and learn a good deal about a dispute over mooring fees. Nobody wants to give hours to a stranger who is obviously asking about hours.

leads.label: Pay somebody to name the collector
leads.description: There is always a man in the lower market who knows which gentleman has been overpaying, and he is always more expensive than he looks.
leads.successText: A name, an address of sorts, and the shape of the order: one leaf, from one set of notes, described so precisely that whoever placed it had read them.
leads.failureText: Your money buys a name that turns out to belong to a fishmonger, and the pleasure of being told so afterwards by three separate people.

leads.label: Sit on the house from the coffee room opposite
leads.description: A night in a window seat with a cold cup, watching who comes back to a house where a man died with the door bolted.
leads.successText: At half past ten a young man tries the street door, finds it sealed by the police, stands in the rain long enough to be certain nobody is inside, and walks away towards the Tussock — the wrong way for a man who lives across it.
leads.failureText: Six hours, four cups, and a great deal of rain. Whoever was coming back had the sense not to come back tonight.

leads.label: Read the university and parish records
leads.description: Who matriculated with whom, who was sent down, and who has been signing for reading-room books he has no business with. All of it public, if you know which clerk to be polite to.
leads.successText: Kohler Fels left the history faculty owing two terms' fees, and has signed the restricted reading room's book four times this year under a supervisor who retired in the spring.
leads.failureText: The clerk is willing and the index is not. You lose an afternoon to a filing system that changed hands in the fifties and never recovered.

leads.label: Read up on divination by plumb and thread
leads.description: Old Neil's shelf has four books on divination by suspended weight. Three of them are wrong in ways he enjoys explaining, and the fourth is the reason the other three exist.
leads.successText: The thread is not the instrument; the thread is the leash. A plumb that keeps pointing after it has been set down is not answering the diviner any more. It has found something nearer to answer.
leads.failureText: You read for a whole evening and come away with a headache, a bibliography, and the strong impression that the useful book is the one Old Neil has not put on the shelf.
